strapline: Nakacinda walks out of Chimbokaila, a US$1.6 billion fertiliser bet in Chilanga, 859 road deaths in a quarter — and a stoppage-time heartbreak for the Copper Princesses

stories.title: Twelve months to the day: Raphael Nakacinda walks out of Chimbokaila after serving his defamation sentence, with a sedition count still to be ruled on in November
stories.excerpt: The Patriotic Front secretary general was released from Lusaka Central Correctional Facility on the morning of Wednesday 21 October, a year after he surrendered to begin an 18-month sentence for defaming President Hichilema. News Diggers and the Zambian Observer report that statutory remission cut the term to twelve months. Supporters in green carried him from the gates; a separate charge of seditious practices returns to the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court on 2 November.

image.label: Out of Chimbokaila
image.caption: PF secretary general Raphael Nakacinda was released from Lusaka Central Correctional Facility on Wednesday 21 October after serving a sentence for defaming the President.

body: Raphael Nakacinda, secretary general of the Patriotic Front, left Lusaka Central Correctional Facility — the prison Lusaka calls Chimbokaila — at about 09:00 on Wednesday 21 October, News Diggers reports. He had been in custody since 21 October 2025, when he surrendered to begin an 18-month sentence with hard labour for defaming President Hakainde Hichilema. The Zambian Observer reports that statutory remission for good behaviour reduced the term to twelve months, which is why his release fell one year to the day after he went in.

The conviction arose from remarks made between 18 and 22 April 2022, in which, according to News Diggers, Mr Nakacinda accused the President of interfering with the judiciary. The Zambian Observer’s account is that he alleged Mr Hichilema was summoning judges to his private residence to influence cases involving the PF. Lusaka magistrate Irene Wishimanga convicted him in May 2024, the Observer reports, and the Lusaka High Court upheld the conviction in October 2025. Criminal defamation of the President was repealed in December 2022; the courts held that the law still applied because the offence predated the repeal.

According to the Zambian Observer, PF supporters and members of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance gathered from dawn, many in party green, and lifted Mr Nakacinda onto their shoulders when he emerged. The Observer describes him as looking slightly thinner than when he went in.

body.text: Prison has not broken us; it has only refined our resolve.
body.attribution: Raphael Nakacinda, PF secretary general, to supporters outside Lusaka Central Correctional Facility on Wednesday 21 October, as reported by the Zambian Observer

body: He went on, in words carried by the Observer, to say that he and his allies had entered the gates as “prisoners of justice” and emerged “ready to breathe fire to challenge this administration”. The ruling UPND’s position, as the Observer summarises it, is that Mr Nakacinda’s cases are matters of law and order rather than political persecution, and that the judiciary acted independently.

body.text: What else is on his file

body: The defamation term was not the only sentence he served. The Observer reports that in December 2025 Principal Magistrate Idah Phiri handed him a further six months with hard labour for hate speech over remarks about voters in Bweengwa, ordered to run concurrently, so that it did not lengthen his stay. News Diggers refers to hate-speech charges brought in 2023 over remarks about Tonga-speaking people without stating the outcome.

One matter remains open. Both outlets report that a count of seditious practices against him returns to the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court on 2 November; News Diggers says the court is due that day to rule on whether he has a case to answer. The Observer alone adds that he was convicted of a separate seditious-practices charge in August 2026, relating to statements about law-enforcement operations, and paid a K2,400 fine rather than serve more time; Lusaka Brief has not found that reported elsewhere.

body.title: Key dates, as reported
items: 18–22 April 2022 — the remarks about the President and the judiciary (News Diggers)
December 2022 — criminal defamation of the President repealed (Zambian Observer)
May 2024 — convicted by magistrate Irene Wishimanga (Zambian Observer)
21 October 2025 — surrenders after the High Court upholds the conviction (Zambian Observer)
December 2025 — concurrent six-month hate-speech sentence (Zambian Observer)
21 October 2026 — released from Chimbokaila (News Diggers, Zambian Observer)
2 November 2026 — ruling due on the seditious-practices count (News Diggers, Zambian Observer)

body.confirmed: That Mr Nakacinda was released on Wednesday 21 October after serving a sentence for defaming the President, and that a seditious-practices count returns to court on 2 November, is reported by both News Diggers and the Zambian Observer. The 18-month sentence, the 2022 remarks and the upholding of the conviction in October 2025 are reported by both.
body.unverified: The August 2026 sedition conviction and K2,400 fine, the Bweengwa hate-speech sentence and the remission arithmetic come from the Zambian Observer alone. News Diggers’ full account is behind its paywall. No statement from the PF or the Government on the release had been published by either outlet at the time of writing.

stories.title: A US$1.6 billion second act in Chilanga: Hichilema breaks ground on the UCF urea expansion and warns officials who slow projects that he will be ‘ruthless’
stories.excerpt: President Hichilema broke ground on Tuesday 20 October for the second phase of United Capital Fertilizer’s ammonia and urea plant in Chilanga, a US$1.6 billion expansion that the company and the President say will lift direct jobs from 7,400 to 10,000. He used the occasion to tell public officers that delays to investment approvals would not be tolerated in his second term.

image.label: Phase two at Chilanga
image.caption: United Capital Fertilizer’s US$1.6 billion second-phase ammonia and urea plant at Chilanga is intended to replace imported fertiliser and employ 10,000 people directly.

body: On Tuesday 20 October President Hakainde Hichilema turned the first soil for the second phase of United Capital Fertilizer’s plant at Chilanga, south of Lusaka. The expansion is valued at US$1.6 billion, according to Open Zambia, the Zambian Observer and Lusaka Times, and will add ammonia and urea capacity — Lusaka Times also lists ammonium nitrate — to a complex the company says already employs 7,400 people directly. The target after the expansion is 10,000 direct jobs, a figure the President used in his speech, with thousands more indirect jobs for transporters, dealers and traders.

Open Zambia and the Zambian Observer report the claim that the completed plant would be the second-largest fertiliser facility in Africa. Lusaka Times reports that UCF has pledged to invest up to US$5 billion in Zambia by 2030 and that the President expects that target to be met early. Chinese ambassador Han Jing, quoted by Lusaka Times, put total investment in the wider industrial park at more than US$3 billion and said the park already provides over 10,000 jobs, and that the first phase has begun trial production.

The President tied the plant to the Government’s production targets — 10 million tonnes of maize, three million tonnes of soya beans and one million tonnes each of wheat and sugar, as the Zambian Observer records them. He argued that none of those targets is reachable without affordable fertiliser made in Zambia, and that domestic production of D compound and urea would cut import dependence, lower input costs and earn foreign exchange, with UCF already a net exporter to the region, Open Zambia reports.

body.text: None of this is achievable without a reliable supply of affordable fertiliser, made in Zambia.
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, at the UCF groundbreaking in Chilanga on Tuesday 20 October, as reported by the Zambian Observer

body: Zambia Monitor reports that the President used the same platform to attack administrative delay. He said approvals for projects and investments that drag on for months or years cost jobs, that he did not need the popularity of “5,000 people” but had to satisfy 21 million Zambians, and that “this president in this second term will be ruthless about these issues”. He urged citizens to “shout” when they see public officers delaying projects. Zambia Monitor notes that he named no specific officials or projects, and no response from the civil service had been reported.

Lusaka Times, whose report was published on the morning of Wednesday 21 October and describes the ceremony as taking place that day, also quotes the President praising UCF’s recycling of groundwater as a model for industry under climate change, and the ambassador calling the groundbreaking “tangible proof of commitments taking root”. Zambia Monitor and the Zambian Observer both date the ceremony to Tuesday 20 October, which is the date used here.

body.title: The numbers, as reported
items: US$1.6 billion — second-phase investment (Open Zambia, Zambian Observer, Lusaka Times)
7,400 → 10,000 — direct jobs now and after expansion (Open Zambia, Zambian Observer)
US$5 billion by 2030 — UCF’s stated investment pledge (Lusaka Times)
10 million tonnes of maize, 3 million tonnes of soya — national targets cited by the President (Zambian Observer)

stories.title: ‘Not the rainfall of 1964’: a regulator tells the Insaka that Zambia’s tailings dams are not ready for three million tonnes of copper a year
stories.excerpt: At the Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka in Lusaka, the Minerals Regulation Commission’s inspections chief said tailings management standards remain inadequate and called for a national registry and independent engineering oversight. Konkola Copper Mines, meanwhile, told News Diggers it has spent US$500 million on its tailings leach plant with US$600 million more committed.

image.label: Tailings on the agenda
image.caption: Regulators at the Mining and Investment Insaka in Lusaka warned that Zambia’s tailings dam standards lag behind its copper ambitions.

body: Zambia’s plan to mine three million tonnes of copper a year came up against the question of what to do with the waste at the Zambia Mining and Investment Insaka this week. Elite Mhone, Director of Mine Inspections and Audits at the Minerals Regulation Commission, told a plenary session that the country’s tailings dam management and safety standards remain inadequate, Lusaka Times reported on Wednesday 21 October. Tailings facilities, unlike water dams, keep growing as waste accumulates, he said, and heavier rainfall under a changing climate raises the risk of failure.

body.text: The size of rainfall we receive now is not the same as rainfall that was being received in 1964.
body.attribution: Elite Mhone, Director of Mine Inspections and Audits, Minerals Regulation Commission, at the Mining and Investment Insaka in Lusaka, as reported by Lusaka Times

body: Mr Mhone called for stricter inspections, independent engineering oversight, a national tailings dam registry and greater accountability for operators. Constantino Mweembela, acting Director of Licensing and Compliance at the Zambia Environmental Management Agency, urged companies to invest in real-time monitoring, follow international tailings standards and work with communities on shared water, saying environmental impact assessments “must go beyond regulatory compliance”. Dr Chikusela Sikazwe of Seed Global Health asked that health be built into impact assessments from the start, to avoid duplicated or under-used clinics.

At its exhibition stand, Konkola Copper Mines presented itself as committed to safe and sustainable mining. Sibongile Kanyungu, the company’s head hydrogeologist at No. 4 Shaft, told News Diggers that KCM has spent US$500 million on its Tailings Leach Plant and committed a further US$600 million, and described her own job as forecasting where underground water will be found and removing it before it endangers operations. The rest of her remarks sit behind the paper’s paywall.

Lusaka Times also reports on a networking evening at the Mulungushi International Conference Centre at which Botswana’s Minister of Minerals and Energy, Bogolo Kenewendo, and the DRC’s Minister of Mines, Louis Kabamba, recommitted with Zambia to connected infrastructure and cross-border value chains — Ms Kenewendo calling for commitments to become “tangible projects”. Acting Minister of Mines Gilbert Siame said the gathering of more than 1,500 participants, which closes on Friday 23 October, should produce deals that serve the target of three million tonnes of copper a year by 2031.
Lusaka Brief reported the Botswana and DRC proposals, and the President’s ‘use it or lose it’ warning to licence-holders, in its edition of Wednesday 21 October.

stories.title: Posters, not practitioners: Lusaka’s mayor says his crackdown on illegal adverts is not aimed at traditional healers, after their association asks him to tread carefully
stories.excerpt: Mayor Chitambala Mwewa says Lusaka City Council will intensify the removal of unauthorised advertising on public infrastructure, including posters promising instant wealth, and that offenders face fines. Dr Rodwell Vongo of the Traditional Health Practitioners Association of Zambia has urged caution on spiritual matters while backing action against unregistered healers, Phoenix News reports.

image.label: The poster war
image.caption: Lusaka City Council says it will remove unauthorised adverts across the city, including those promising miraculous wealth, and insists traditional medicine itself is not the target.

body: A dispute over who may advertise what, and where, on Lusaka’s streets has drawn in the city’s traditional healers. In a statement made available to Smart Eagles on Wednesday 21 October and carried by the Zambian Observer, Mayor Chitambala Mwewa said Lusaka City Council would step up enforcement against unauthorised and misleading advertisements on public infrastructure and in undesignated areas. Offenders face removal of their materials, fines and other penalties under council regulations; the statement does not name a by-law or a fine.

The mayor was responding to remarks by Dr Rodwell Vongo, president of the Traditional Health Practitioners Association of Zambia, which the council said it had “noted with concern”. Videos circulating online had shown the mayor removing healers’ posters, Phoenix News reports. Mr Mwewa’s position is that traditional medicine is part of Zambia’s heritage and is not the target; the council removes political posters and commercial adverts in the same way, and exempting spiritual adverts would itself be discriminatory.

body.text: Our concern is not with spirituality or personal beliefs, but with the legality of the advertising medium.
body.attribution: Chitambala Mwewa, Mayor of Lusaka, in a statement to Smart Eagles on Wednesday 21 October

body: He singled out adverts promising instant wealth, guaranteed success or miraculous outcomes that cannot be verified, saying they may exploit vulnerable people, and referred to reported cases of young people led to believe that wealth could come through criminal or ritual acts. All advertisers, he said, should obtain approvals and make claims that are truthful and lawful.

Dr Vongo, speaking to Phoenix News in a report carried by the Zambian Observer, asked the mayor to handle spiritual matters with an understanding of “the spiritual realm” rather than from a purely physical standpoint — while commending his effort to bring order to the city. He said his association supports measures to protect citizens and hold lawbreakers to account, condemned recent reported killings linked to promises of wealth, and offered to work with the Government to identify people falsely posing as practitioners. He urged the public to beware of unregistered healers.
Neither report gives figures for posters removed or fines issued, and the council’s statement does not say when the intensified enforcement begins.

sources.title: Lusaka Mayor warns of stiff penalties for illegal advertisers, clarifies that the council’s crackdown is not targeting traditional healers or traditional medicine

stories.title: 859 dead in three months: police count 12,865 road crashes between July and September, up 27 per cent on last year, as a head-on collision near Zimba kills two Americans
stories.excerpt: Zambia Police recorded 12,865 road traffic accidents and 859 deaths in the third quarter of 2026, against 10,126 crashes and 753 deaths in the same period of 2025, spokesperson Chipo Kaitisha said on Wednesday. Lusaka had almost half the crashes. The evening before, a Fortuner and a Hino collided on the Great North Road south of Zimba, killing two American passengers.

image.label: The third-quarter toll
image.caption: Zambia Police’s third-quarter figures show 12,865 crashes and 859 deaths between 1 July and 30 September 2026, with speeding the most-cited cause.

body: Zambia’s roads killed 859 people between 1 July and 30 September 2026, according to figures released by Zambia Police spokesperson Chipo Kaitisha in Lusaka on Wednesday 21 October and reported by Zambia Monitor and News Diggers. Police recorded 12,865 road traffic accidents in the quarter: 747 fatal, 1,202 causing serious injury, 2,706 causing slight injury and 8,210 involving only damage to property. A further 2,144 people were seriously hurt.

The comparison with the third quarter of 2025 is stark. Crashes rose from 10,126 to 12,865, an increase of 2,739 or about 27 per cent, Zambia Monitor reports; fatal crashes rose from 583 to 747 and deaths from 753 to 859. Road traffic offences recorded went up only slightly, from 49,564 to 50,100, while revenue from admission-of-guilt fines fell from about K22.6 million to about K19.2 million.

Lusaka Province accounted for 6,325 of the crashes, nearly half the national total, followed by the Copperbelt with 2,378 and Central Province with 1,194; Northern Province recorded the fewest at 252. Police attribute most crashes to human error, with excessive speed cited 3,014 times, misjudging clearance distance 1,897 times, failing to keep to the nearside 1,571 times, cutting in 1,231 times and ignoring signs and signals 1,163 times.
Children under 16 were among 560 casualties, of whom 91 died and 186 were seriously injured; most were pedestrians or passengers. There were 410 hit-and-run crashes, 68 of them fatal.

body.text: The impact of accidents on children under the age of 16 remains a major concern.
body.attribution: Chipo Kaitisha, Zambia Police spokesperson, in a statement issued in Lusaka on Wednesday 21 October, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: Ms Kaitisha said the police would step up road-safety campaigns and enforcement, and urged drivers to avoid speeding, drink-driving and phone use, to keep vehicles roadworthy and to wear seat belts.

The statistics were released the day after a crash that illustrates the most common of those causes. At about 17:40 on Tuesday 20 October a Toyota Fortuner travelling south and a Hino Ranger travelling north collided head-on at Sky Layby on the Great North Road, about 10 km south of Zimba in Southern Province, Lusaka Times reports. Two American passengers in the Fortuner, both aged 67, died at the scene; their bodies are at Zimba Mission Hospital awaiting post-mortem examination. Eight people were injured and taken to Livingstone University Teaching Hospital. Southern Province Commanding Officer Moono Namalongo said in a statement to ZANIS that the Hino driver had attempted to overtake improperly while travelling uphill, and reminded drivers to be sure the road ahead is clear.

stories.title: Drilling for a virus on the doorstep: Luapula tests its Ebola response with mobile laboratories as Nigeria becomes the fifth country with a case from the DRC outbreak
stories.excerpt: The Zambia National Public Health Institute ran a simulation in Milenge district this week to see how fast mobile laboratories can be deployed and return Ebola results, Zambia Monitor reports. The exercise comes as the World Health Organization confirms an imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in Abuja, Nigeria, with 44 contacts under watch, and as Kenya counts nine cases.

image.label: Milenge drill
image.caption: Zambia’s public health institute tested the deployment of mobile Ebola laboratories in Milenge, Luapula Province, on the border with the DRC.

body: Luapula Province, which shares a long border and many communities with the Democratic Republic of Congo, has been the site this week of a national test of Zambia’s readiness for Ebola. Zambia Monitor reports that a delegation from the Zambia National Public Health Institute conducted a simulation exercise in Milenge district to assess how quickly mobile laboratories can be deployed and how fast they can return test results. ZNPHI acting director general Dr Nyambe Sinyange said the drill is part of national preparedness for the outbreak in the DRC, and that testing the plan in advance would expose gaps and strengthen coordination.

Luapula permanent secretary Prudence Chinama-Kangwa, receiving the delegation, called for stronger surveillance and cross-border cooperation, and said the mobile units would enhance the province’s ability to detect and respond promptly. The laboratories, worth US$1.7 million, were provided with United States support, according to US defence attaché Lieutenant Colonel Matt Yan; the exercise also involved the Defence Force Medical Services, the Disaster Risk Management Division and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, whose country director Diane Morof said it would check that laboratory results are accurate as well as prompt.

body.text: Swift and coordinated action will be critical to containing any potential Ebola case and preventing further transmission.
body.attribution: Dr Wamunyima Chingumbe, Director General of Defence Force Medical Services, at the Milenge exercise, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body.text: The outbreak the drill is for

body: The World Health Organization’s Africa office said on Tuesday 20 October that Nigeria had confirmed an imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in Abuja — the fifth country to detect the virus since the DRC declared its outbreak on 15 May 2026. The patient, a woman with recent travel to Uganda, fell ill on 7 October, sought care at a private facility on 11 October and was confirmed positive on 20 October; 44 contacts are being monitored. Kenya has reported nine cases linked to an imported case in recent weeks, WHO said.

Zambia Monitor, citing Uganda’s health ministry, reports that the woman had travelled on business to eastern DRC and only transited Uganda, and that investigators have yet to establish where she was infected. The same report puts the outbreak at more than 9,500 infections and over 4,600 deaths and says WHO has called it the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak on record; Lusaka Brief has not verified those totals against a WHO page.

WHO’s advice to countries in the region is to keep surveillance strong, have laboratories ready to test safely, pre-position supplies, engage communities and heighten monitoring at points of entry — while advising against restrictions on travel to or trade with affected countries. Neither report describes any new measures at Zambia’s own border posts.

stories.title: Two Public Procurement Act convictions in a week: Chongwe’s district health director fined K330,000 over contracts to his own company; a former Solwezi council officer jailed
stories.excerpt: Chongwe Resident Magistrate Francis Sato found Dr Mweene Nseluke guilty on ten counts of failing to declare a conflict of interest and fined him K330,000 on Monday 19 October, the Anti-Corruption Commission said in a statement reported by Zambia Monitor. News Diggers reports that the Solwezi Subordinate Court has separately jailed a former municipal council officer for three months over a K100,000 procurement.

image.label: Conflicts declared late
image.caption: The Anti-Corruption Commission has announced two convictions under the Public Procurement Act within days of each other, in Chongwe and Solwezi.

body: The Anti-Corruption Commission has secured two convictions in a week for public officers who did business with their own offices. In Chongwe, Resident Magistrate Francis Sato on Monday 19 October found Dr Mweene Nseluke, 47, the district health director, guilty on all ten counts of failing to declare a conflict of interest, Zambia Monitor reports. The charges were brought under sections 19(3)(b) and 19(9), read with section 107, of the Public Procurement Act No. 8 of 2020.

The court heard that Dr Nseluke approved payments and personally withdrew funds under a contract for servicing and repairing Ministry of Health vehicles in Chongwe district, with the money going to Lukem Prominent Ventures, a company in which he had a direct interest. He was fined a total of K330,000, payable within 14 days, failing which he faces prison terms of between three and 24 months on the various counts, to run concurrently.

The ACC arrested Dr Nseluke in June 2025. At that time News Diggers reported the alleged sum at more than K422,000 and said he had been released on bond ahead of a plea on 20 June 2025. The Commission’s head of corporate communications, Joseph Mwenya, confirmed the conviction in a statement in Lusaka on Wednesday 21 October, saying the Commission “reiterates that public office must never be exploited for personal gain”. Neither report records any response from Dr Nseluke or his lawyers, nor whether he intends to appeal.

News Diggers reports that the Economic and Financial Crimes Division of the Solwezi Subordinate Court has sentenced a former Solwezi Municipal Council officer to three months’ simple imprisonment and a K70,000 fine for contravening the Public Procurement Act. According to the ACC statement quoted by the paper, she had bid through her own business for council contracts to supply petunia flowers, cleaning materials and stationery worth about K100,000, and was arrested in July 2025. Mr Mwenya said the conviction should serve as a deterrent to public officers tempted by unlawful procurement practices. The paper’s full report is behind its paywall; no second outlet had named the officer in the reports found for this edition, so she is not named here.

body.confirmed: The Chongwe conviction, the ten counts, the K330,000 fine and the 14-day payment deadline are reported by Zambia Monitor from an ACC statement; the June 2025 arrest and the alleged K422,000 were reported by News Diggers at the time. The Solwezi sentence is reported by News Diggers from the same ACC spokesperson.
body.unverified: No second outlet had carried either conviction at the time of writing, and neither report includes a response from the convicted officers. Whether either will appeal is not reported.

stories.title: Ahead twice, beaten in the 100th minute: the Copper Princesses lose 3–2 to Venezuela and go into Saturday’s match with France without a point
stories.excerpt: Elizabeth Mofya and Grace Phiri each put Zambia in front in Morocco on Wednesday night, but Venezuela equalised twice and Andrea Suárez scored the winner in the tenth minute of stoppage time — one of the latest goals in the tournament’s recent history. Zambia sit bottom of Group D on zero points and face France on Saturday 24 October. On Friday, Red Arrows defend a 1–0 lead against Kaizer Chiefs in Durban.

image.label: Two leads, no points
image.caption: Zambia’s under-17 women led Venezuela twice but lost 3–2 to a goal in the 100th minute at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup in Morocco.

body: Carol Kanyemba had asked her under-17s to turn the 5–0 defeat by Japan into a comeback against Venezuela. For 99 minutes on Wednesday 21 October they very nearly did. Elizabeth Mofya scored in the fourth minute, Venezuela’s Ariana Ojeda levelled on 13 minutes, Grace Phiri restored Zambia’s lead early in the second half, Orliany Durán equalised again after the hour — and then, with the tenth added minute almost gone, Andrea Suárez struck the winner. Venezuela 3, Zambia 2, Africa Top Sports and CONMEBOL report; ESPN lists the venue as Salé, beside the capital Rabat.

CONMEBOL notes that the Suárez goal, timed at 99 minutes 41 seconds, was the second-latest in the last five editions of the tournament, and that Venezuela remain unbeaten against African sides at this level, having now beaten Zambia twice and Cameroon once. It was the first time this year Venezuela had come from behind to win.

Japan, who have won both their matches, lead the group on six points; France and Venezuela have three each; Zambia have none, with a goal difference of minus six, according to the standings carried by ESPN. The final round is on Saturday 24 October, when Zambia play France and Venezuela play Japan. The top two in each of the six groups go through to the round of 16 with the four best third-placed teams, so the Princesses are not yet mathematically out, but they would need a win and a favourable set of results elsewhere.

Before the match Ms Kanyemba told reporters that the lesson of the Japan game was compactness — “we were marking in isolation” — and that “defeat in the tournament is not the end of the tournament”, ZamFoot reports. No post-match comments from the Zambian camp had been published at the time of writing.

Red Arrows carry a 1–0 lead from Ndola into the second leg of their CAF Confederation Cup qualifier against Kaizer Chiefs on Friday 23 October at Moses Mabhida Stadium in Durban, kick-off 18:00. Alassane Diarra’s header from a corner, shortly after Chiefs’ 71st-minute substitutions at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium on Saturday 17 October, decided the first leg, AfricaSoccer reports. The winners over two legs reach the group stage, where CAF’s minimum prize money is US$400,000 and the matches run from 27 November to 24 January, according to the same site, which also notes that Arrows played in Ndola because Nkoloma Stadium does not meet CAF requirements.

stories.title: Thirty-two hours, 214 kilometres and the last lap alone: Cosmas Bwalya sets a Zambian record at the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship at York Farm
stories.excerpt: Cosmas Bwalya won Zambia’s leg of the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship at York Farm in Lusaka with 32 laps, or 214.6 km, beating the previous national best of 30 laps, News Diggers reports. Runner-up Alick Mashowo also passed the old mark with 31 laps, and Bwalya may now qualify for the 2027 individual world championship in Tennessee.

image.label: Lap thirty-two
image.caption: Cosmas Bwalya ran 32 hourly laps, 214.6 km in all, to win Zambia’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship race at York Farm and set a national record.

body: A backyard ultra has no finish line, only a bell. Every hour, on the hour, the runners set off on a loop of 6.7 km; anyone who fails to be back and ready for the next start is out, and the race ends when one person completes a lap that nobody else does. At York Farm in Lusaka this week that person was Cosmas Bwalya, who ran his 32nd lap alone to win Zambia’s race in the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, News Diggers reports — 214.6 km over 32 hours.

The previous Zambian best, according to the results cited by the paper, was 30 laps, set by Winstone Mwale. Bwalya was not the only runner to pass it: Alick Mashowo finished second on 31 laps (207.9 km), also beyond the old record, and Joseph Mumba was third on 24 laps. The paper’s full report, including the field size and the conditions, is behind its paywall, and it does not give the race dates.

The team championship format sees each country’s runners compete simultaneously at home, with national totals compared across the world. News Diggers reports that Bwalya’s tally may qualify him for the 2027 Backyard Ultra World Individual Championship in Tennessee in the United States, subject to confirmation by the organisers. No comment from Bwalya himself appears in the visible portion of the report, and the paper does not say how Zambia’s combined total compares with other national teams in the championship.
The result adds a second Zambian sporting footnote to a week otherwise dominated by football: Lusaka Brief reported on Wednesday that Ken Sekeletu had retained his boxing title in Tenerife.

sources.title: Bwalya sets national record at Backyard Ultra World Championship

stories.title: Forty years of NATAAZ: the national theatre festival gathers in Chingola, with a K100,000 grant per arts association and a nudge towards the digital stage
stories.excerpt: The National Theatre Arts Association of Zambia is holding its 2026 Senior Festival in Chingola as it marks its 40th anniversary, with the winners expected to feed the theatre nominations for the Ngoma Awards. A speech from the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts told performers to use digital platforms to reach audiences and funders, and said arts associations each received a K100,000 grant this year, Zambia Monitor reports.

image.label: NATAAZ at forty
image.caption: The National Theatre Arts Association of Zambia’s Senior Festival in Chingola marks the association’s 40th anniversary and produces nominees for the Ngoma Awards.

body: Zambia’s amateur and semi-professional theatre companies have converged on Chingola for the 2026 Senior Festival of the National Theatre Arts Association of Zambia, an event that this year doubles as the association’s 40th anniversary, Zambia Monitor reports. The festival is sponsored by Konkola Copper Mines and the Zambia National Service, and its results are expected to produce the nominees for the theatre category of the Ngoma Awards, alongside winners from the intermediate category for colleges and universities.

The Government’s message to the stage was delivered by Esther Ngambi, Director of Arts, reading a speech on behalf of Kangwa Chileshe, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts. It urged artistes to use digital platforms to put their work before wider audiences and to attract funders and partners, and restated support for theatre and the wider arts sector.

body.text: The government supported arts associations in 2026 with grants of K100,000 each to strengthen their operations and activities.
body.attribution: Kangwa Chileshe, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts, in a speech read at the NATAAZ Senior Festival in Chingola, as reported by Zambia Monitor

body: Chingola district commissioner Howard Kamwandi encouraged artists to apply to the Constituency Development Fund for creative enterprises, particularly projects that create jobs. Maureen Lilanda, chairperson of the National Arts Council of Zambia, asked theatre practitioners to “focus on adding value to their discipline” and to position themselves to contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda — a phrase echoed by NATAAZ chairperson Moses Mtonga, who thanked the Government for its support.
Zambia Monitor’s report does not give the festival’s dates, the number of companies competing or the productions staged, and the awards had not been announced at the time of writing.

sources.title: Artistes urged to embrace digital platforms to expand reach, funding

analysis.title: What Nakacinda’s release changes, and what the 2 November ruling could still change
analysis.body: Raphael Nakacinda went into Chimbokaila a year ago as the secretary general of a party in opposition; he comes out into a landscape in which, as this week’s reports describe it, PF supporters march alongside the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance and the question of who leads the opposition in Parliament has only just been settled by the Speaker. His supporters’ reading, voiced at the gate, is that the sentence was political and that his return reinvigorates the opposition. The ruling party’s reading, as the Zambian Observer summarises it, is that an independent court applied a law that was still in force when the offence was committed. Both can point to the record: the conviction survived appeal, and the law it rested on was repealed in December 2022. What remains live is the seditious-practices count on which the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court rules on 2 November. A finding that there is a case to answer puts him back in the dock within weeks of his release; a finding that there is not would leave him without a pending case for the first time in years. Watch, too, for whether the PF formally restores him to his full duties, and for any statement from the party or the Government, since neither had published one by Thursday morning.

analysis.title: The fertiliser plant is a bet on import substitution. Three things will tell if it pays
analysis.body: A US$1.6 billion expansion that takes a single company from 7,400 to 10,000 direct jobs fits the Government’s stated logic: grow maize to ten million tonnes, and do it with fertiliser made in Chilanga rather than imported. Whether the bet pays will show up in three places. First, the price farmers actually pay: import substitution lowers input costs only if domestic urea is sold below the landed import price, and none of this week’s reports says what UCF will charge, or on what terms it supplies the Farmer Input Support Programme. Second, the feedstock: the President’s remark, reported by Lusaka Times, that coal can produce the ‘white stuff’ points to a coal-based process, and the reports do not address what that means for emissions or for coal supply. Third, the timetable: the first phase has only begun trial production, according to the Chinese ambassador, and the company’s US$5 billion-by-2030 commitment is a pledge rather than a contract. The President’s warning that he will be ‘ruthless’ with officials who delay approvals is aimed at the third of these. The first two will decide whether the plant changes what a bag of fertiliser costs a smallholder.

analysis.title: Why a drill in Milenge matters more than a case in Abuja
analysis.body: Nigeria’s first Ebola case is alarming because of distance: the virus travelled from eastern DRC to a private clinic in Abuja before anyone tested for it. Zambia’s risk runs the other way — not distance but proximity. Luapula shares border communities with the DRC, as its permanent secretary noted this week, and the outbreak declared on 15 May has already produced cases in Kenya and now Nigeria. That is why this week’s simulation in Milenge matters more to Zambians than the headline from Abuja. The question the exercise was built to answer is simple: how many hours between a suspected case in a border village and a laboratory result? Mobile laboratories, if they work as intended, shorten that gap, and the US$1.7 million of US-funded units are the tool. What the reports do not yet tell us is the result of the drill — where the gaps were, and what will be fixed. Nor do they say whether monitoring at Zambia’s border posts has been stepped up since the Nigerian confirmation, which WHO’s guidance on points of entry would support even as it advises against trade or travel restrictions. Those are the follow-ups to watch for from ZNPHI and the Ministry of Health.
